item.title: Psychotherapy's Hidden Secrets
item.description:
Therapy

Psychotherapy's Hidden Secrets

Does psychotherapy include the transmission or teaching of esoteric secrets?

Posted July 25, 2026

Key points
  • Modern society's complexity and chaos may be driving increased collective psychological distress.
  • There is a deep hunger for existential and spiritual guidance beyond quick symptom fixes.
  • Much psychotherapeutic wisdom seems enigmatic, precious, and shielded from public view.
Freud's famous couch.
Source: JRennocks/Wikimedia Commons/CC BY 4.0

This post is Part 1 of a series that will examine the nature of what I refer to as clinical wisdom and provide specific examples of some of these esoteric secrets of psychotherapy.

How much of what we call psychotherapy is about the teaching or transmission of certain esoteric and well-guarded secrets about psychology, life, and how to best live it? What are some of these secrets? Where do they come from? And exactly how would such profound and transformative "clinical wisdom" be conveyed from clinician to client or patient? These are difficult questions. Difficult because there are so many (400 to 500) different types of psychotherapy practiced today with diverse approaches, goals, techniques, and methods.

Most contemporary therapies are strictly symptom-centered, while some are more concerned about treating the whole person (holistic) and promoting personal growth and, perhaps, spiritual development. And there are, of course, various and very different reasons that people seek psychotherapy in the first place, though, for most, it is the painful or debilitating presence of psychiatric signs and symptoms. (See my prior post.)

But if I could distill the primary reason for the continuing existence, and recent resurgence, of psychotherapy as a practice and profession, and what mainly motivates someone to seek it, it would generally come down to this: the universal or archetypal experience of suffering and the perennial problem of evil. We may not be fully conscious of what truly causes us to seek psychotherapy, but rumbling beneath the surface are profound philosophical, existential, and spiritual questions: Why do we suffer? Why is there evil in the world? Does life have meaning? Is there free will? What am I responsible for in life? Why must we die? Is there anything beyond death? Why do I feel so alone? Who am I? Why am I here? What is my purpose or significance? What do I really want, and how can I get it?

We are currently not only in an age of miraculous technological, scientific, and medical advances that enable us to live longer and better, stay more closely linked with others and world events, and enjoy access to modern marvels such as computers, cell phones, television, the internet, GPS, and AI; but, at the same time, we find ourselves in an equally unprecedented period of frustration, rage, hostility, hatred, chaos, alienation, and confusion. Twenty-first-century existence is becoming more complex, stressful, and difficult to manage. Racism, sexism, misogyny, genocide, antisemitism, fascism, terrorism, mass shootings, political animosity, and, more generally, human evil—an archaic concept coming back into use by some psychologists, psychiatrists, sociologists, and the public connoting those pernicious attitudes and actions that promote excessive interpersonal aggression, violence, and disregard for the rights of others—are escalating alarmingly around the world. As C.G. Jung (1961) prophetically observed, “Evil has become a determinant reality. It can no longer be dismissed from the world by a circumlocution. We must learn to handle it, since it is here to stay. How we can live with it without terrible consequences cannot for the present be conceived.”

article continues after advertisement

Consequently, our collective mental health is suffering. These chronically traumatic conditions take a devastating toll on the psyche, spirit, and soul. The incidence of serious psychiatric disorders is on the upswing. Suicide rates in the U.S. over the past two decades rose by 25 percent. According to the National Institutes of Mental Health, more than 44 million Americans suffer from some sort of serious psychiatric symptoms such as depression, panic attacks, generalized anxiety, bipolar disorder, and psychosis. This staggering statistic excludes an additional 20 million who are living with substance use disorders. Indeed, we remain in the unremitting grip of a runaway opioid abuse epidemic, indicative of the futile and dangerous desire to anesthetize (via substance use, alcoholism, workaholism, or problematic behaviors surrounding food or sex or technology) our psychological suffering and escape from stark existential reality at all costs.

People are discouraged, distressed, disoriented, and desperate to make sense of their lives, to find purpose and meaning, peace of mind, self-esteem, security, belonging, power, recognition, and significance, and to discover new and more constructive ways of coping with the perturbing and perilous vicissitudes of post-pandemic existence. But sadly, they seldom possess the necessary skills, means, and knowledge to do so on their own. Yet, there exists, as I contend in my new book, a vast treasure trove of what I call "clinical wisdom," painstakingly accrued, conserved, curated, and protected by countless psychotherapy practitioners over the past century, that is desperately needed in our day and, therefore, far too precious to stay secret.

Psychotherapy—the therapeutic treatment of mental disorders, existential suffering, and human misery utilizing psychological methods and, perhaps surprisingly to some, more meaningfully defined as healing of the soul or mind—has, in some form or another, been practiced now for more than a century by medical and mental health professionals around the world. Ever since the famed Viennese physician Sigmund Freud, the undisputed father of modern psychotherapy, first introduced the revolutionary “talking cure” and controversial treatment method he called “psychoanalysis,” generations of psychotherapy patients have been privy to a rich and varied collection of clinical wisdom aimed at alleviating, or at least mitigating, their suffering and setting them on the path toward healing and wholeness. Yet, for the most part, it remains enigmatic and shrouded in mystery.

To be sure, the theory and practice of psychotherapy have dramatically evolved since Freud's day, but all these changes have only added to the diverse wealth, breadth, richness, mystique, and complexity of the potent clinical wisdom it can convey. Over the past decade, and particularly during and since the COVID-19 pandemic, the prevalence and availability of psychotherapy have grown significantly. And as for how psychotherapy is now provided, in 2025, the global use of online video therapy—a relatively recent development in the delivery of psychotherapy services, popularized during the pandemic—will likely exceed $65 billion annually. Psychotherapy has become big business. This is because now, more than ever, we need the encouragement, insight, and inspiration that the cumulative clinical wisdom of psychotherapy can provide. As Jung (1961) himself succinctly said, "Today we need psychology [and psychotherapy] for reasons that involve our very existence." His words ring doubly true in these deeply unsettling, terrifying, and troubled times.

article continues after advertisement

Indeed, despite dubious trends in recent decades toward a more superficial neurobiological, pharmacological, and cognitive-behavioral approach to the understanding and treatment of psychiatric disorders, and, in effect, a demystifying or mechanization of therapy, there remains a profound, pervasive, and palpable personal and collective hunger for real psychological, philosophical, and spiritual guidance, knowledge, and wisdom. We need to recognize this pervasive psychological, philosophical, and spiritual longing, this intense craving for meaning and purpose, this festering soul-sickness from which we individually and collectively suffer today, and provide in psychotherapy pragmatic clinical wisdom to help restore our soul, strengthen our self, and sustain our sanity in a sometimes seemingly insane world.

item.title: When Should AI Enter the Classroom?
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

When Should AI Enter the Classroom?

Early use of generative AI can narrow student solutions and hinder metacognition.

Posted July 25, 2026

Key points
  • AI adds the most value when it comes after a first attempt at thinking, not before it.
  • Groups with immediate AI access consistently converged on strikingly similar solutions.
  • The deeper challenge is not only timing AI correctly, but keeping students the authors of their own thinking.

Co-authored by Paul Surlis, Ava Gilmartin, and Michael Hogan.

Imagine a group of postgraduate students who have just been handed a complex water management problem. Their challenge is to develop a sustainable water management plan for a busy tourist city, balancing environmental protection, economic growth, and increasing demand for scarce resources.

Working in small teams, they have ninety minutes to understand the problem, debate possible solutions, and agree on a plan. Within minutes, several groups begin consulting ChatGPT. By the end of the session, each group submits a polished proposal. Although the groups never interacted with one another, many of their solutions are strikingly similar: in their structure, in the assumptions they make, and in the possibilities they never explore. Nothing has been copied. Yet something important has been lost.

This is the scene that lies behind a recent study by Romero (2025). As generative AI becomes an increasingly familiar part of higher education, the most important question may no longer be whether students should use AI at all. A more useful question is when AI should enter the learning process. Could introducing AI too early erode the very creativity, discussion, and cognitive effort that universities are trying to cultivate?

Testing the Impact of AI Introduction Timing

To test whether timing really mattered, Romero (2025) designed a simple but revealing experiment. Thirty-six graduate students were randomly assigned to one of three conditions while working in small groups on the water management challenge. One group had access to ChatGPT from the very beginning. A second group spent the first fifteen minutes working without AI, debating ideas, questioning assumptions, negotiating different perspectives, and building an initial solution together, before AI was introduced later as a tool for refinement. A third group completed the task entirely without AI. Although this was a relatively small quasi-experimental study involving a single task, its design isolated one variable that is often overlooked in discussions about AI in education: timing.

The results were striking. Groups with immediate access to AI consistently converged on similar solutions, suggesting that early reliance on AI narrowed idea diversity and encouraged familiar lines of thinking rather than independent exploration. By contrast, students who first grappled with the problem themselves generated a broader range of ideas before using AI to challenge, extend, and refine their thinking. Interestingly, the groups that never used AI produced the most diverse solutions, although their work was also more variable in quality. Romero (2025) draws an important design principle from this: AI appears to be most valuable when it enters as a finishing tool rather than a starting point.

Romero's (2025) study involved just thirty-six students completing one collaborative task, meaning the findings should be viewed as early evidence rather than definitive proof. Yet the pattern is a suggestive one. By delaying AI, educators may be protecting a period of productive cognitive struggle before technology begins shaping students' thinking. That naturally raises a deeper question: why should fifteen minutes without AI make such a difference?

When AI use Leads to Metacognitive Laziness

Fan et al. (2025) offer a compelling explanation by examining what happens inside learners' thinking when AI becomes part of the learning process.

In a randomised experiment involving 117 university students, participants completed a two-stage English reading and writing task before revising their work with one of four forms of support: ChatGPT, a human expert, a structured writing checklist, or no additional support. Researchers then used trace data to map how students regulated their own learning during the revision process - what they monitored, what they evaluated, when they paused to orient themselves.

The ChatGPT condition centred students' self-regulatory process on the AI. Interactions were extensive. Essays improved. But compared with the human expert and checklist conditions, the ChatGPT group showed relatively fewer of the metacognitive processes — evaluation and orientation — that involve stepping back, assessing where you are, and deciding what to do next. Human expert support triggered transitions between orientation and evaluation that ChatGPT simply did not. And crucially, when knowledge gain and transfer were measured, not just task performance alone, the ChatGPT group’s advantage disappeared.

This is what Fan et al. call metacognitive laziness: not laziness in the everyday sense, but the subtle displacement of the self-regulatory thinking that makes learning stick. The connection to Romero is direct: reaching for AI immediately risks skipping the period of struggle and genuine cognitive effort that precedes good ideas. Romero shows what this costs in terms of creative diversity. Fan et al. show what it costs in terms of metacognitive development. Together, the studies point towards the same educational principle: giving students time to think before introducing AI may help preserve both.

Creativity researchers have long recognised that good ideas rarely appear the moment a problem is presented. Instead, they emerge through something closer to Wallas's (1926) classic four-stage sequence of preparation, incubation, insight, and verification. The incubation stage, where people continue thinking without immediately reaching for an answer, is often where unexpected connections begin to form. The delayed access condition in Romero's study can be understood as a pedagogical attempt to protect that incubation space, which might otherwise never open at all.

From pedagogical timing to personal habit

If delaying AI helps preserve the thinking that underpins creativity and learning, the next question is how educators should design for it. Romero's study cannot tell us whether fifteen minutes is enough, or whether the same principle applies across different subjects, learning activities, or assessment formats. Those questions remain open. Timing is only one design decision. Educators must also consider which tasks genuinely benefit from AI, how assessment can reward thinking rather than polished output, and how learning activities can scaffold the metacognitive processes that AI may otherwise displace.

Ultimately, the deeper challenge is designing learning environments in which students remain the authors of their own thinking. Getting the timing right is one important step. Preserving learners' agency as AI becomes a permanent feature of education may prove to be the much larger task. However, agency cannot indefinitely depend on pedagogical structures that merely delay access to AI. As students encounter AI beyond carefully designed classroom activities, they will increasingly need to regulate their own use of these tools.

This means developing practical habits of good AI use: generating ideas before prompting, critically evaluating AI suggestions, and using AI to extend rather than replace their own thinking. In this sense, agency is not simply self-regulation, but self-regulation guided by an understanding of how to sustain learning over the long term. As AI becomes a permanent feature of education, the quality of learning may increasingly depend on the opportunities students are given to think before they prompt. Yet these habits do not emerge automatically. Educators play a central role in cultivating them through thoughtful pedagogical design, helping students gradually become capable of protecting their own agency even when external constraints are no longer present.
